event_description: Oklahoma Executive Order 2021-06. From FMCSA's copy: Extreme freezing temperatures and severe winter weather including snow, freezing rain, and wind beginning February 7, 2021, and continuing, are expected to cause damage to public and private properties and utilities
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air had spread into eastern Oklahoma and northwestern Arkansas on the 8th, and gradually deepened across the region. Precipitation began as freezing drizzle across the area on the 8th, with ice accumulation up to .25 of an inch reported in some areas, as the freezing drizzle persisted for 24 to 48 hours. As the cold air deepened, the freezing drizzle became periods of snow flurries and light snow. This was especially true in areas downwind of some of the lakes in northeastern Oklahoma. Lake effect snow produced up to 1.5 inch accumulations in some areas, a rare occurrence indeed for this region.||A strong storm system translated into the Southern Plains from the Southern Rockies on the 14th and 15th. Heavy snow began across the area with the approach of the main storm system during the early morning hours of the 14th. Several rounds of widespread heavy snow produced four to eight inches of accumulation, as the snow continued into the early afternoon hours of the 15th in some areas as the storm system moved away from the region. The heaviest snow fell in a swath along and south of I-44, and north of I-40, across portions of Okfuskee, Creek, Okmulgee, Tulsa, Wagoner, Rogers, Mayes, Cherokee, and Delaware Counties.||In addition to the heavy snow, much of eastern Oklahoma experienced excessively cold wind chill from the 14th through the 16th. Temperatures fell below zero across the area on 15th and 16th, and wind chill values were as low as -20 to -30 degrees.

event_description: Oklahoma Executive Order 2021-06. From FMCSA's copy: Extreme freezing temperatures and severe winter weather including snow, freezing rain, and wind beginning February 7, 2021, and continuing, are expected to cause damage to public and private properties and utilities
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historic outbreak of arctic air resulted in record breaking cold temperatures during an extreme cold spell that lasted almost two weeks for some locations across the combined Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. The cold air moved over the northeastern combined Panhandles as early as Feb 8th, and spread southwest through Feb 12th, engulfing most of the southern plains by Feb 13th. The northeast Panhandles remained below freezing for 12 days straight while the southwest Panhandles were below freezing for a full week or more. Periods of flurries and freezing fog also occurred mainly in the overnight and morning periods almost each day Feb 8th through Feb 18th. In addition, two storm systems interacted with the arctic air to produce several inches of snow, not only across the Panhandles but across most of the Great Plains, including almost the entire state of Texas and surrounding states. ||The frigid arctic air would put a strain on area power grids, resulting in rotating blackouts for some locations (this was much worse for other portions of Texas due to a state wide power crises felt most on the ERCOT power grid). The extreme cold also caused multiple indirect fatalities in the Texas Panhandle and led to school closings due to winter weather and/or the Texas energy crises that required measures to strongly limit energy consumption. The cold also halted plant operations due to issues with natural gas fuel, killed some livestock and also caused localized damage to residences and schools due to freezing water pipes. There were isolated reports of private water wells freezing up across the area. In addition, several municipal water wells in the southeast Texas Panhandle froze up and sustained damage (Donley County) during this time. There was also reported damage to water treatment facilities in Oldham County.||While local impacts in the Panhandle were less than the rest of Texas because the region's infrastructure is more built to handle major cold outbreaks, losses in the state of Texas were estimated to be well into the billions. Impacts from the power disruptions and natural gas fuel issues caused by the cold were certainly felt well outside of the worst hit areas and this included the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. For example, local dairy production was halted for a period of time because the processing plants located outside the Panhandles were without power and unable to operate. Farmers were forced to dispose of milk produced during this timeframe. Damage outside the Panhandles to the southeast was extensive due to power interruptions within the ERCOT power grid which led to numerous broken pipes and damages down state in Texas. These greater disruptions impacted the far southeast Texas Panhandle, which was the only area that was included on the ERCOT power grid at the time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Exact start times of wind chills below -15��F were not possible to get as mesonet sites across the Oklahoma Panhandle were frozen from below freezing temperatures and freezing fog since the 8th of February in Beaver County. It is estimated that winds were well above 15 mph which accompanied by temperatures in single digits to below 0��F . Wind chill values got as low as -15 to -30 between the morning of the 14th through the late morning to afternoon of the 15th. Though this was the most dangerous time period to be exposed to the elements. Areas in the county endured below freezing temperatures for around 306 hours straight, almost 13 full days. The coldest ambient temperature reading at the Beaver mesonet was -15 ��F on the 15th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historic outbreak of arctic air resulted in record breaking cold temperatures during an extreme cold spell that lasted almost two weeks for some locations across the combined Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. The cold air moved over the northeastern combined Panhandles as early as Feb 8th, and spread southwest through Feb 12th, engulfing most of the southern plains by Feb 13th. The northeast Panhandles remained below freezing for 12 days straight while the southwest Panhandles were below freezing for a full week or more. Periods of flurries and freezing fog also occurred mainly in the overnight and morning periods almost each day Feb 8th through Feb 18th. In addition, two storm systems interacted with the arctic air to produce several inches of snow, not only across the Panhandles but across most of the Great Plains, including almost the entire state of Texas and surrounding states. ||The frigid arctic air would put a strain on area power grids, resulting in rotating blackouts for some locations (this was much worse for other portions of Texas due to a state wide power crises felt most on the ERCOT power grid). The extreme cold also caused multiple indirect fatalities in the Texas Panhandle and led to school closings due to winter weather and/or the Texas energy crises that required measures to strongly limit energy consumption. The cold also halted plant operations due to issues with natural gas fuel, killed some livestock and also caused localized damage to residences and schools due to freezing water pipes. There were isolated reports of private water wells freezing up across the area. In addition, several municipal water wells in the southeast Texas Panhandle froze up and sustained damage (Donley County) during this time. There was also reported damage to water treatment facilities in Oldham County.||While local impacts in the Panhandle were less than the rest of Texas because the region's infrastructure is more built to handle major cold outbreaks, losses in the state of Texas were estimated to be well into the billions. Impacts from the power disruptions and natural gas fuel issues caused by the cold were certainly felt well outside of the worst hit areas and this included the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. For example, local dairy production was halted for a period of time because the processing plants located outside the Panhandles were without power and unable to operate. Farmers were forced to dispose of milk produced during this timeframe. Damage outside the Panhandles to the southeast was extensive due to power interruptions within the ERCOT power grid which led to numerous broken pipes and damages down state in Texas. These greater disruptions impacted the far southeast Texas Panhandle, which was the only area that was included on the ERCOT power grid at the time.

Storm total snowfall amounts were generally four to eight inches across much of northeastern and east-central Oklahoma, with locally up to ten inches reported.

This resulted in hazardous travel conditions mainly on bridges and overpasses, as well as some secondary roadways. ||An observer 7 ESE of Ringold measured one-quarter inch of ice, with another observer 1 SW of Idabel also measuring one-quarter inch of ice. An observer near Battiest measured 0.4 inches of snow from this event.

event_description: Oklahoma Emergency Order # 2022-26. From FMCSA's copy: I hereby declare (in the context of the State of Emergency due to extreme drought conditions as outlined in Executive Order No. 2022-23)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued across McCurtain County in Southeast Oklahoma throughout October. This was in response to an extended flash drought that resulted from an exceptionally hot and dry month in June with below normal rainfall in what is historically one of the wettest months on average. This was followed up by an even hotter and drier month in July with the total rainfall amounts for July generally around an inch or less, which was only near 25% of normal. Near normal rainfall occurred in August, but hot and dry conditions returned in September with below normal rainfall while much of October remained below normal until beneficial rainfall returned late in the month, promoting some improvements in drought. This dryness contributed to lower than normal streamflow observed across area creeks, streams, and rivers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Long term drought conditions continued to keep rangelands grassless putting a strain on ranchers, which have been forced to supplement feed or sell off cattle. Soil moisture continued to be short to very short for portions of the combined Panhandles through October. These soil conditions slowed the planting of winter wheat for some areas in the more extreme to exceptional drought conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Much of the county started the month off in Extreme Drought (D3) to Exceptional Drought (D4) with a small portion of the far west and southeastern corner of the county were in Severe Drought (D2). Over the course of the month conditions continued to degrade with half of the county ended the month in D4 and the other half in D3. The area of D4 remained across central portions of the county surrounded by D3 in the west and east. The county ended the month 1 to 2.5 below normal for October Rainfall. The county remains in an 8 to 12 deficit year to date.

event_description: Oklahoma Memo to OEM 2-26-23 Severe Weather
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful storm system, with highly anomalous magnitudes of wind shear and moisture for late February, impacted the forecast area on the evening of the 26th. A broken line of severe thunderstorms developed across the eastern Texas Panhandle/far western Oklahoma and quickly swept through much of the forecast area. Widespread wind damage, including gusts near 90 mph, along with a record number of tornadoes (13) for February occurred. Several reports of large hail were also received. Behind the line of thunderstorms, a tight pressure gradient and strong westerly low-level jet allowed widespread 50-60 mph winds gusts to continue through the late evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado northwest of Amorita significantly damaged a barn. This tornado may have persisted longer, but no additional damage was observed in this very rural area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous upper level system passed over the southern Great Plains on Sunday February 26th, 2023. This brought widespread strong winds and blowing dust to the Panhandles, particularly during the late afternoon and evening hours as a Pacific cold front rapidly moved eastward, with the large amount of dust leading to greatly reduced visibility and treacherous driving conditions. East of this front, severe thunderstorms developed which led to two tornadoes in the southeastern Texas Panhandle and additional damaging winds.

event_description: Oklahoma Memo to OEM 2-26-23 Severe Weather
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent upper-level trough progressed from the Four-Corners Region into the Texas Panhandle by late in the afternoon on March 1st and through March 2nd. Strong warm and moist air advection was ongoing in advance of the trough preceding the event. This resulted in scattered convection, but this had little effect on increasing instability through the afternoon as temperatures warmed into the mid and upper 70s to lower and mid 80s. This environment produced an isolated strong thunderstorm that produced nickel size hail just south of Haworth on the 1st. A potent upper-level trough progressed from the Four-Corners Region into the Texas Panhandle by late in the afternoon on March 2nd. Strong warm and moist air advection was ongoing in advance of the trough earlier in the morning. This resulted in scattered convection, but this had little effect on increasing instability through the afternoon as temperatures warmed into the mid and upper 70s to lower and mid 80s. Additionally, backing surface winds also promoted increasing low-level shear as well as deep-layer shear with a 50-60 knot low-level jet surging east ahead of the trough and advancing cold front. This environment was supportive of several supercells that developed by late afternoon into the early evening hours, producing an isolated tornado in addition to large hail and damaging wind gusts Across McCurtain County Oklahoma. As the cold front surged east of I-35 by early in the evening, the storm mode eventually became more linear with an increasing threat of more widespread damaging winds along the complex of storms while the threat of large hail also continued through the end of the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nickel size hail reported just south of Haworth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably warm temperatures, high wind, and low relative humidity combined with dormant fuels to promote conditions that supported the rapid spread of wildfire across portions of eastern Oklahoma in mid to late March. Two direct fatalities were attributed to fires in Pawnee and Haskell Counties, where homes were burned.

event_description: State of Emergency - Cleveland, Creek, Dewey, Grady, Lincoln, Logan, Oklahoma, Pawnee, Payne, Pottawatomie, Roger Mills, and Stephens counties (wildfires and straight-line winds beginning March 14, 2025)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably warm temperatures, high wind, and low relative humidity combined with dormant fuels to promote conditions that supported the rapid spread of wildfire across portions of eastern Oklahoma in mid to late March. Some of the worst wildfires occurred on the 14th, with near record warm temperatures, very dry air behind a dry line, and very strong wind gusting to near 70 mph locally. Numerous wildfires occurred during this period, some of the largest of which burned almost 32000 acres, 115 homes, and 145 outbuildings in Pawnee County, more than 6500 acres in Latimer County, about 3000 acres in Adair, Haskell and Pittsburg Counties, more than 2000 acres in Pushmataha County, about 1700 acres in Sequoyah County, about 1200 acres in Delaware and Cherokee Counties, nearly 1000 acres in Le Flore County, and over 400 acres in Creek County. Two direct fatalities were attributed to fires in Pawnee and Haskell Counties, where homes were burned.

event_description: State of Emergency - Cleveland, Creek, Dewey, Grady, Lincoln, Logan, Oklahoma, Pawnee, Payne, Pottawatomie, Roger Mills, and Stephens counties (wildfires and straight-line winds beginning March 14, 2025)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level system brought in high winds early in the day on the 14th and stuck around through the afternoon.   Breezy southwest surface winds shifted to the west with the arrival of a Pacific front. Behind this front much stronger winds aloft started to mix to the surface. Winds started gusting above 58 mph almost immediately behind the front with a ground station near Bootleg, TX measuring a gust of 59 mph at 5:10 AM CDT. Two other stations near Romero and Adrian, TX measured a gust of 60 mph at 5:22 AM CDT. As the day started to warm up with the sun out, much higher winds started to mix to the surface along with sustained winds pickin up into the 35 to 50 mph range. The south central and southwestern TX Panhandle saw their winds peak between 1030 AM and 230 PM where some areas to the north like the OK Panhandle and to the east winds did not peak until later in the afternoon. Some of the highest winds measured were 84 mph at the mesonet station in Hereford and 83 mph measured by the Amarillo Airport ASOS around 10:43 AM CDT. These high winds quickly caused blowing dust with visibility issuse especially around the southern TX Panhandle. The high winds created problems for high profile vehicle such as tractor trailors or semi-trucks but also caused dangerous travel conditions with reduced visibilities falling below 1/4 mile. With winds being westerly this especially caused problems along I-27 south of Amarillo which runs north and south causing mutliple semi-trucks to overturn. ||Dry air which over took the Panhandles during the afternoon also combined with the high winds creating a high fire danger day. Multiple fires impacted the combined Panhandles with a couple of these fires impacting residents of around Alanreed and McLean, Texas as Fire Warnings had to be issued to prepare folks for the potential of an evacuation. One fire impacted campers at Wolf Creek Park southeast of Perryton, TX. This fire also closed down a section of HWY 70 south of Perryton.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Each observation site had multiple high wind gusts ranging from 58 mph to 66 mph.

Many locations across the Oklahoma Panhandle observed wind gusts o 60mph or greater. These strong winds brought blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions as well. EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Ranger Road fire ignited during the morning of February 17th near Highway 64, one mile southeast of Beaver, Oklahoma. This fire burned 283,283 acres across Oklahoma and Kansas. The fire was fueled by dormant, dry grasses and brush, driven by wind gusts of 60-70 mph and extremely low humidity (10-15%). These conditions created a fast fire environment, allowing the blaze to explode in size���growing from ignition to 15,000 acres in one hour to over 145,000 acres in just nine hours. It rapidly crossed the state line into Clark, Comanche, and Meade counties in Kansas. With strong wind gusts, this helped not only to spread the fire but limited aerial firefighting operations and complicated suppression efforts during the first stages of the fire's expansion. The cause is undetermined.  A firefighter was injured from being burned. In addition, a fire truck from Rosston Fire overturned in Beaver County and three fire fighters were injured, including one that suffered from 2nd and 3rd degree burns and broke his leg. There were 926 primary homes, 2 schools, and commercial/government buildings threatened. Evacuations: Mandatory evacuations for about 771 people that may have covered KS as well.  Gate and Knowles had evacuations on Feb 17th, and numerous outbuildings were destroyed in the fire.

event_description: State of Emergency - Beaver, Texas, and Woodward counties (wildfires)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of McCurtain County Oklahoma through the month of February. Rainfall amounts during February only tallied to 1.50-2.50 inches,  which was only half or less the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought had expanded across the southern half of McCurtain County during the final few weeks of the month.

event_description: Alfalfa, Creek, Grant, Major, Okmulgee, Rogers, Tulsa, and Wagoner
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and northern Oklahoma from the late evening of the 5th into early morning hours of the 6th. This activity developed in the vicinity of a dryline as a deep upper trough began to establish across the Four Coners. As a nocturnal low-level jet strengthened after sunset, a pair of cyclic tornadic thunderstorms emerged from the eastern Texas Panhandle into northern Oklahoma. In addition to several tornadoes, including a deadly tornado west of Fairview in Major County, large hail and eventually damaging wind gusts were observed with severe convection across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado developed about 4 miles west-southwest of Helena, or about a mile southeast of the community of McWillie. This tornado moved generally northeast although there was some variability in motion as it moved north of Helena and then south and east of Jet. Power poles were damaged as the tornado crossed State Highway 45 and areas west of Helena. Significant damage was observed along State Highway 58 north of Helena where a number of power poles were broken along a mile stretch of SH-58, and at least three barns were destroyed (EF2) both along SH-58 and east of SH-58 on E0300 Road. The tornado continued to produce tree and power pole damage as it moved northeast. Power poles were broken east of Jet along N2740 Road and along U.S. Highway 64 on both sides of the Alfalfa-Grant County line.  The tornado then moved into Grant County with the centerline crossing the county line just north of U.S. 64.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An estimated wind gust near the intersection of U.S. Highway 60 and Streetman Road. The report was relayed by emergency management.

The High School and Middle School roof sustained significant damage, and the bus barn also suffered heavy damage to the roof and overhead doors. This strongest and widest phase of the tornado occurred as it moved east along Grimes Road. One single-wide manufactured home was completely destroyed and several other single-family residences were heavily damaged with the loss of roofs and windows. Two fatalities and two injuries occurred at one homestead, where a double-wide manufactured home was completely destroyed and several automobiles were moved and tossed 20 to 30 yards. A nearby barn was destroyed and heavy limb loss occurred on large trees. The tornado then continued northeast, crossing Highway 75, where it threw a metal shipping container across the lanes and uprooted trees. The tornado dissipated after crossing North 205 Road, about three miles south of the Tulsa County line. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 135 to 145 mph. The tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KINX WSR-88D.

An emerging upper trough and sharp dryline facilitated development of scattered intense supercell thunderstorms across portions of northern Oklahoma, with reports of large to very large hail, thunderstorm wind damage and several tornadoes. In addition to a family of well-documented tornadoes from east of Medford, Oklahoma (Grant County) to near Braman, Oklahoma (Kay County), a violent tornado impacted areas around Vance Air Force Base and the south/east extents of Enid, Oklahoma. This tornado prompted a rare Tornado Emergency, the first in the WFO Norman Forecast Area since May 19th, 2024.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Enid Tornado initially developed near or on the southwest portion of Vance Air Force Base and moved east-northeast crossing over the southern edge of the runway complex, but remaining south of the majority of structures on the base. However as the tornado crossed US-81, it moved through the Gray Ridge Estates neighborhood where most of the houses in the neighborhood sustained damage, and many destroyed or receiving significant damage. Damage to at least three homes in this neighborhood was rated EF4. ||After moving northeast out of this neighborhood, the tornado moved through open land. Although the tornado continued moving through areas without structures, damage done to trees east of Leona Mitchell Blvd and north of Fox Drive was significant. At least one tree was debarked, and a hardwood tree was pulled from the ground and displaced 20 feet to the east. Farther northeast, significant ground scouring and severe tree damage was observed as the tornado crossed E0455 Road and South 16th Street. At Southgate Road, a number of structures were destroyed including two metal buildings, a warehouse and an outbuilding. An RV parked in this area was picked up and the chassis of this RV was found about 305-310 yards northeast of its origination point. Damage was rated EF4 in this area as well.||The tornado moved through more open land damaging trees as it approached S 30th Street. Radar and damage patterns indicate that the tornado moved in a loop briefly just southwest of South 30th Street and Rupe Road. A home was destroyed (EF4) and a number of other structures and trees were destroyed or heavily damaged along South 30th Street. Coming out of the loop, the tornado moved southeast across S 30th Street thereby continuing in relatively open land as opposed to moving northeast toward a d neighborhood on the southeast side of Enid. A farmstead was hit at S 42nd Street and Rupe Road destroying a barn, damaging the house and trees on the property.||Crossing Rupe Road, radar indicated the tornado likely moved in a loop again northeast of Rupe Road and S 42nd Street, before moving southeast and east and dissipating near Boggy Creek just west of Woodring Airport.||Despite the intensity of this tornado, there was only one injury that required transport.||Scientific notes: Researchers at the National Severe Storms Laboratory and the University of Illinois performed a variety of calculations to estimate the potential wind speed of the tornado. Two researchers performed a treefall pattern analysis to match the observed pattern of treefall to a simulated pattern from a vortex model. One researcher used this method to determine a probabilistic wind speed distribution from treefall near Southgate Road using six different sets of constraints. The calculated median maximum 3-second velocity in all of these six experiments was over 205 mph, and the interquartile range of two of these six experiments was completely over 200 mph. ||A second researcher also performed a treefall analysis with a Monte Carlo simulation slightly adjusting the input variables. Taking the runs with the lowest 0.5% error, a median estimated maximum wind velocity of 94 m/s (210 mph) was calculated.||A third researcher made calculations of the 300 yard displacement of the RV near Southgate Road using simulations with a 3-dimensional vortex model that does include modeled vertical motion of the tornado, again using a Monte Carlo simulation. Of the simulations that provided the closest match the displacement of the RV, the maximum winds of these simulations were 91-97 m/s (204-217 mph).||Based on these engineering calculations that included both 3-dimensional vortex modeling (including vertical motions) and 3-second averaging wind speed averaging consistent with the EF-scale values, it is very highly likely that this tornado produced winds that would be classified as an EF5 tornado in the vicinity of Southgate Road.

event_description: Garfield and Kay
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another widespread thunderstorm and severe weather period impacted the southern one-half of Oklahoma and adjacent north Texas on the evening of the 25th. This event included several supercell thunderstorms across this area, including a cyclic tornadic supercell that moved in areas south of Wichita Falls, Texas into Archer and Clay Counties. Several other (generally brief) tornadoes occurred with storms across south-central and southeastern Oklahoma, though signal of residual inhibition and numerous storm interactions on the cool side of a quasi-stationary boundary generally limited low-level mesocyclone organization and longevity. Large hail and sporadic wind damage also occurred with storms across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

event_description: Garfield and Kay
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite a rather volatile airmass for severe weather across Oklahoma and north Texas on the 26th, misaligned synoptic features (i.e., neutral-to-rising mid-level heights) and remnant convective inhibition limited the overall number/coverage of thunderstorms during the evening. The most significant storm was a slow-moving supercell storm near and north of Wichita Falls, Texas. This thunderstorm produced large to very large hail and yielded a pair of left-moving supercells that went on to produce hail into portions of adjacent southern Oklahoma. This included confirmations of baseball-size hail in areas east of Lawton, Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING. The event time was adjusted based on radar observations.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Braman Tornado: Numerous spotters and chasers observed this tornado develop in western Kay County. The initial damage occurred near 140th Street and Earth Road where a tree was uprooted and a farm house suffered roof damage. The tornado continued generally east breaking a power pole on 124th Street south of Earth Road and destroying a barn and damaging more power poles and trees near Earth Road east of 124th Street. The first of two satellite tornadoes developed in this area near Earth Road between 124th and 108th. The primary tornado moved north, then looped back around to an easterly movement as the motion of both the primary tornado and the satellite tornado was influenced by the Fujiwhara effect.||As the primary tornado moved east-northeast after this interaction, a barn was destroyed along Earth Road east of 108th Street, and a number of trees and power poles were damaged along 76th Street near Fork Road. As the tornado was crossing the Chickaskia River, a second satellite tornado developed and rotated around this primary tornado. The tornado continued east snapping power poles along 60th Street, and destroying two barns and more power poles along 44th Street just south of the city limits of Braman. The survey and mobile radar data from the Doppler on Wheels project show that the tornado made another loop just southeast of Braman and east of US-177, then moved southeast damaging trees along Fork Road east of 29th Street before dissipating.

event_description: Garfield and Kay
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and through the evening on April 24th as a cold front advanced from Southeast Oklahoma into the Ark-La-Tex. Intersecting this front was an outflow boundary, which moved west southwest out of Arkansas toward Northeast Texas and Northern Louisiana. This same boundary was slow in advancing and showed signs of stalling across Southeast Oklahoma just ahead of the cold front. Low-level shear in this area was sufficient to support strong updrafts with 0-1 km storm-relative helicity (SRH) over 100 m2/s2. The air mass was very moist and unstable with deep-layer shear around 50 knots, further aiding storm longevity. As a result, an isolated severe thunderstorm across northeast McCurtain County produced large hail in the Cottage community east of Smithville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to quarter size covered the ground in the Cottage community east of Smithville.

event_description: Garfield and Kay

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail ranging from dime to nickel size reported near the Felker community between Valliant and Wright City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another widespread thunderstorm and severe weather period impacted the southern one-half of Oklahoma and adjacent north Texas on the evening of the 25th. This event included several supercell thunderstorms across this area, including a cyclic tornadic supercell that moved in areas south of Wichita Falls, Texas into Archer and Clay Counties. Several other (generally brief) tornadoes occurred with storms across south-central and southeastern Oklahoma, though signal of residual inhibition and numerous storm interactions on the cool side of a quasi-stationary boundary generally limited low-level mesocyclone organization and longevity. Large hail and sporadic wind damage also occurred with storms across the region.
